behavior_items: The reproducer defines a function template `run(Funct funct = Funct())` that takes a callable object by value and immediately invokes it as `funct(1)`. In the call site, template argument deduction instantiates `Funct` as the unique closure type of a lambda expression, and the default argument is not used because an explicit lambda argument is supplied.

Inside `runner()`, a local `std::vector<int> vec = {1};` is created and then captured by reference with `[&]` in the lambda passed to `run`. The lambda therefore stores a reference to the local vector object in `runner`, and `run` copies that closure object by value into its parameter `funct` while preserving the reference member semantics.

The lambda has a generic call operator because its parameter is `const auto& num`. When `run` executes `funct(1)`, the lambda's templated `operator()` is instantiated with `num` bound to an `int` temporary through `const int&`. This exercises C++20 generic lambda template instantiation and immediate invocation through a copied closure object.

The lambda body performs `vec.back() = num;`. Since `vec` initially contains one element `{1}`, `vec.back()` yields a valid reference to the last element, and assignment writes `1` back into that element. Semantically the vector remains `{1}` after the call, so the program's observable value is unchanged.

After the call to `run`, `runner()` returns `vec` by value from inside the `try` block. This requires the compiler to model the lifetime and state of a local object that was referenced and mutated through a lambda closure before being returned. Optimization can encourage constant evaluation, inlining, and aggressive reasoning about the returned object state.

The presence of `try { ... } catch (...) {}` is important because it introduces exception-handling control flow around the vector construction, lambda invocation, and return path. The compiler must represent both the normal path returning `vec` and the exceptional path returning `{}` after the catch. This complicates optimization and constexpr-style object/state analysis.

`main()` calls `runner()`, stores the returned vector, and prints `vec.back()`. Under correct compilation, the returned vector is non-empty and its last element is `1`, so the program should print `1`. There is no intended undefined behavior on the normal path exercised by the source.

According to the bug report, the failure is not a user-program error but a GCC internal compiler error that appears only with optimization enabled (`-Ox`) and only in C++20/C++23 modes on GCC 14/15. This indicates the reproducer is triggering an optimizer/front-end interaction rather than producing wrong runtime semantics in the source itself.

The reported ICE location `cxx_eval_indirect_ref` in `cp/constexpr.cc` shows GCC is attempting constexpr-style evaluation of an indirect reference expression during compilation. Even though the program is not explicitly `constexpr`, modern optimization and front-end analysis can reuse constant-expression machinery to reason about temporary objects, lambda captures, member access, and return values.

The key expression pattern likely stressing the compiler is an indirect access through a lambda-captured reference into a non-trivial standard library object, specifically `vec.back()` on a local `std::vector<int>` captured by reference and invoked through a generic lambda passed as a template argument. That combines closure copying, reference capture, templated call operator instantiation, library member access, and mutation of a local object.

The reproducer is minimized enough that removing optimization, changing the language mode before C++20, or simplifying the control/data flow likely avoids the buggy compiler path. This strongly suggests the regression is tied to newer C++20 front-end evaluation rules or implementation changes in GCC 14 that affect how the compiler symbolically evaluates the lambda/reference access pattern.

In short, the code exercises: template argument deduction for a closure type, generic lambda instantiation, by-value passing of a closure holding references, mutation of a local vector via `back()`, return-by-value of that vector across a `try`/`catch`, and subsequent use of the returned value. GCC's crash means it mishandles this combination during compile-time analysis under optimization, not that the source has invalid runtime logic.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer is a valid C++20 program whose normal behavior is straightforward: `runner()` creates a one-element `std::vector<int>`, passes a reference-capturing generic lambda to a template function `run`, the lambda writes `num` into `vec.back()`, `runner()` returns the vector, and `main()` prints `1`. The interesting part is the compilation path it forces: GCC must instantiate a generic lambda closure type, copy that closure into a template parameter while preserving a reference capture to `vec`, analyze the mutation `vec.back() = num`, and then reason about returning the mutated local vector from inside a `try` block with a catch-all fallback. Under `-Ox` and `-std=c++20`/`c++23`, GCC 14/15 appears to route this through constexpr evaluation machinery (`cxx_eval_indirect_ref` in `cp/constexpr.cc`) and crashes with an internal compiler error. So the reproducer primarily exercises a regression in GCC's compile-time analysis of indirect reference access through a generic lambda capture into a local `std::vector` across optimized exception-aware control flow.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern points to a GCC front-end/constexpr-evaluation regression rather than a problem in user code. The ICE occurs only with optimization and only in C++20/C++23, which strongly suggests an optimization-enabled semantic analysis path introduced or changed for newer language modes. The crashing function `cxx_eval_indirect_ref` indicates GCC is trying to symbolically/constexpr-evaluate an indirect reference expression while analyzing code that is not explicitly `constexpr`. The triggering construct is a generic lambda copied into a function template parameter, with the lambda capturing a local `std::vector<int>` by reference and mutating it through `vec.back() = num`. That requires GCC to model a copied closure object containing a reference capture, instantiate the generic lambda call operator for `int`, dereference the captured reference, and track mutation of a non-trivial library object that is later returned by value. The surrounding `try`/`catch` adds EH control flow, so the compiler must merge normal and exceptional paths while preserving object state. A likely common pattern is mishandling of indirect references to captured objects during compile-time object-state evaluation, especially when the referenced object is a non-trivial class and the access occurs through inlined generic lambda machinery under optimization.
possible_causes: Bug in `cp/constexpr.cc` handling of indirect references (`INDIRECT_REF`/reference binding) for lambda captures by reference, causing `cxx_eval_indirect_ref` to see an invalid or unexpected representation of the captured `std::vector` object.

Regression in constant-expression/style evaluation of generic lambda `operator()` instantiations in C++20+, especially when the closure object is passed by value but contains reference members, leading to incorrect object identity/lifetime tracking.

Incorrect front-end modeling of a copied closure that preserves reference capture semantics, so optimization/inlining loses the distinction between the closure object and the referenced local variable and later crashes when evaluating member access through that reference.

Failure in GCC's compile-time state tracking for mutation of non-trivial class objects through captured references, specifically member access via `vec.back()` on `std::vector<int>` during symbolic evaluation.

Optimizer/front-end interaction that wrongly routes non-`constexpr` code into constexpr evaluation machinery after inlining/IPA folding, exposing an unhandled path for reference-captured object mutation in lambdas.

Exception-handling path merge bug: the `try`/`catch` around vector construction, lambda invocation, and return may leave constexpr/object-state analysis with inconsistent bindings for the local vector across normal and exceptional exits.

C++20 regression in template instantiation/evaluation of generic lambda parameters bound as `const auto&` to a temporary `int`, combined with reference capture, causing malformed evaluation state for the assignment expression.

Bug in evaluation of member access/call chains on captured references to standard-library containers, where `vec.back()` produces a reference into container state that constexpr analysis cannot safely represent and crashes instead of bailing out.
evidence: Reported ICE site is `cxx_eval_indirect_ref` in `cp/constexpr.cc`, directly implicating GCC's constexpr-style indirect reference evaluation.

Failure depends on `-Ox`; without optimization the reproducer does not crash, indicating the buggy path is triggered by inlining/constant propagation/front-end optimization analysis rather than parsing or basic semantics.

Failure depends on `-std=c++20`/`c++23` and is a GCC 14/15 regression, pointing to newer language-mode handling such as generic lambda/template evaluation changes rather than longstanding container semantics.

The lambda captures `vec` by reference, is copied by value into `run(Funct funct)`, and then invoked immediately; this is exactly the kind of closure/reference indirection that could confuse indirect-reference evaluation.
The lambda is generic (`const auto& num`), so GCC must instantiate templated `operator()` and evaluate the body through an extra template/lambda layer before reaching `vec.back() = num`.
The mutated object is a non-trivial `std::vector<int>` local later returned by value, requiring object-state and lifetime reasoning beyond a simple scalar reference.
The `try`/`catch` introduces EH control-flow joins between normal return of `vec` and fallback return `{}`, increasing the chance of inconsistent symbolic state during analysis.
The source is semantically valid and should print `1`; the observed problem is an internal compiler error, confirming the defect is in GCC production compiler code rather than in the reproducer.

selected_files.reason: The ICE is reported directly in `cxx_eval_indirect_ref` at `cp/constexpr.cc:5954`, making this the primary suspect. The reproducer specifically stresses constexpr-style evaluation of an indirect reference through a copied lambda closure that captures a local `std::vector<int>` by reference, exactly matching the kind of object/reference handling done in this file.

The failing pattern depends on construction and representation of a generic lambda closure with a reference capture, then copying that closure by value into a function template parameter. If the closure object or capture proxy is modeled incorrectly, `cp/constexpr.cc` could later crash when evaluating the captured reference, so lambda lowering/building is highly suspicious.

The reproducer requires instantiating the generic lambda’s templated `operator()` in C++20 mode and threading that instantiation through optimized evaluation. A regression in template instantiation or substitution for generic lambdas could create malformed trees or bindings later consumed by constexpr evaluation.

The problematic expression is reached via a templated call `funct(1)` on a copied closure object, requiring overload resolution, call building, argument binding to `const auto&`, and construction of the lambda invocation tree. If call-building produces an unexpected reference or indirection form, `cxx_eval_indirect_ref` may ICE on it.

The reproducer only wraps the vector creation, lambda call, and return inside `try`/`catch`, and that EH structure is called out as important to triggering the bug. A front-end exception-handling interaction could leave inconsistent object-state or cleanup trees that later hit the constexpr evaluator during optimization.

The bug appears only with optimization, strongly suggesting inlining exposes the problematic lambda/body structure to front-end constant/object-state analysis. Inlining `run` into `runner` would directly expose the copied closure and captured-reference mutation pattern that leads to the ICE.

Optimization-only failures in non-constexpr code can arise when IPA constant propagation/specialization feeds more aggressive folding or symbolic evaluation. Since `run` is tiny and invoked with a known closure object, IPA-CP could help trigger the constexpr-style path that later crashes.

Early or IPA inlining is a plausible enabler for the regression because the reproducer hinges on a very small template wrapper around a lambda call. If the crash depends on the optimizer making the lambda invocation explicit inside `runner`, this file is a plausible contributing source.

Since the node returned is one of the elements of INSTANTIATIONS, callers may store information in the TREE_PURPOSE or TREE_TYPE of the nodes, and retrieve it from the value returned.

If DECL is a specialization of some template, return the most general such template. Otherwise, returns NULL_TREE. For example, given: template <class T> struct S { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int>::f(U)' this will return the full template. This function will not trace past partial specializations, however. For example, given in addition: template <class T> struct S<T*> { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int*>::f(U)' this will return `template <class T> template <class U> S<T*>::f(U)'.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Return the most specialized of the template partial specializations which can produce TARGET, a specialization of some class or variable template. The value returned is a TEMPLATE_INFO; the TI_TEMPLATE is a TEMPLATE_DECL node corresponding to the partial specialization, while the TI_ARGS is the set of template arguments that must be substituted into the template pattern in order to generate TARGET. The result is cached in the TI_PARTIAL_INFO of the corresponding TEMPLATE_INFO unless RECHECKING is true. If the choice of partial specialization is ambiguous, a diagnostic is issued, and the error_mark_node is returned. If there are no partial specializations matching TARGET, then NULL_TREE is returned, indicating that the primary template should be used.

One reason for doing this is a scenario like this: template <class T> void f(const T&, int i); void g() { f(3, 7); } template <class T> void f(const T& t, const int i) { } Note that when the template is first instantiated, with instantiate_template, the resulting DECL will have no name for the first parameter, and the wrong type for the second. If the current function has a cleanup that might throw, and the return value has a non-trivial destructor, return a MODIFY_EXPR to set current_retval_sentinel so that we know that the return value needs to be destroyed on throw. Do the same if the current function might use the named return value optimization, so we don't destroy it on return. Otherwise, returns NULL_TREE. The sentinel is set to indicate that we're in the process of returning, and therefore should destroy a normal return value on throw, and shouldn't destroy a named return value variable on normal scope exit. It is set on return, and cleared either by maybe_splice_retval_cleanup, or when an exception reaches the NRV scope (finalize_nrv_r). Note that once return passes the NRV scope, it's effectively a normal return value, so cleanup past that point is handled by maybe_splice_retval_cleanup.

Generate insns to zero all st registers together. Return true when zeroing instructions are generated. Assume the number of st registers that are zeroed is num_of_st, we will emit the following sequence to zero them together: fldz; \ fldz; \ ... fldz; \ fstp %%st(0); \ fstp %%st(0); \ ... fstp %%st(0); i.e., num_of_st fldz followed by num_of_st fstp to clear the stack mark stack slots empty. How to compute the num_of_st: There is no direct mapping from stack registers to hard register numbers. If one stack register needs to be cleared, we don't know where in the stack the value remains. So, if any stack register needs to be cleared, the whole stack should be cleared. However, x87 stack registers that hold the return value should be excluded. x87 returns in the top (two for complex values) register, so num_of_st should be 7/6 when x87 returns, otherwise it will be 8. return the value of num_of_st.
